chunk_text: Through the Turkish "Health Transformation Program (HTP)", in which comprehensive reform initiatives were put forward under the title "Health for All", efforts were accelerated in parallel with the developments in the world, and changes were made to solve the problems in the health system [1, 2]. With the implementation of the HTP, a people-centered approach has become increasingly significant, prioritizing equitable access to healthcare services while focusing on the individual ben­ eficiary's needs, demands, and expectations [1]. In other words, the patient-centered approach advocated by the HTP elevates the significance of patients in practice, ensures the reshaping of the system with a "people first" mentality, and places the individual at the center of treat­ ment and care services [3, 4]. Thus, health establishments ensure the fulfillment of patient expectations through their emphasis on patient-centered healthcare services and the patient-provider relationship [5]. Patient expectations encompass the characteristics that medical and managerial services provided by health establishments should possess [6], the anticipations regarding the process or outcome of medical care [7], and the expected beliefs and values, constructed based on cognitive processes, regarding healthcare service processes, events, or outcomes [8]. Patient expectations, then, refer to the services or characteristics of services that patients expect to receive from the healthcare deliv­ ery system. Examples include the structure of healthcare services (building, equipment, staff, etc.), healthcare ser­ vice processes (waiting time, staff-patient interaction, etc.), health outcomes (the impact of healthcare service on patient health, patient's self-assessment of health, etc.), and patients receiving services from different branches/departments [9]. Moreover, patient expecta­ tions are not solely limited to those that are recognized or visible; they also include expectations that possess unconscious qualities, which the patient or the doctor may not be fully aware of [10]. As can be seen, the fact that patient expectations vary makes it difficult to estab­ lish a common definition of patient expectations. Expectations are often explained based on accepted theoretical foundations and by developing specific mod­ els for individuals' behaviors. These include Expectancy Theory [11-14], Social Learning Theory [11, 14-16], Social Cognitive Theory [17-23], Social Exchange Theory [24-26], Response Expectancy Theory [27, 28], Assimila­ tion Theory [29], Contrast Theory [30], General Negativ­ ity Theory [29], Assimilation-Contrast Theory [31, 32], and Adaptation-Level Theory [33]. The examined theo­ ries and models offer various solutions to different cir­ cumstances and problems, providing guidance on what to do and how to act. When determining patient expectations, it is crucial to overcome barriers such as disagreements regarding appropriate methods for identifying, monitoring, and classifying events that constitute expectations, wishes, and concerns [34]. For this reason, researchers should prefer expectation theories that are useful for their implementation, relevant to the target audiences they directly engage with, and considerate of their benefit. In this regard, this study aims to deter­ mine the expectations of cardiology clinic patients from the service delivery process. The research question and sub-research questions developed in line with the aim of the study are given below. Research question What are the expectations of people with cardiovascular disease from healthcare services? Sub-research questions: • What are the expectations from the health establishment? • What are the expectations from doctors? • What are the expectations from nurses? • What are the expectations from the treatment and care process? Method Research team and reflexivity All interviews were conducted by the first author (AD), who was the sole researcher present in the field during data collection. The interviewer holds a PhD in health management and has prior training and experience in qualitative research methods. The interviewer was a male researcher. There was no prior relationship between the researcher and the participants before the study. Eligible patients were identified during their hospitalization period, with support from the nursing staff. Patients who expressed willingness to participate were approached directly by the researcher. Prior to the interviews, participants were fully informed about the researcher's academic background, the purpose of the study, data confidentiality, and the voluntary nature of participation. To establish rapport and trust, a brief informal conversation regarding participants' health con­ ditions and personal background was conducted before initiating the interview questions. Written informed con­ sent was obtained from all participants. To minimize researcher bias, data collection and analy­ sis were guided by a predefined literature-based theoreti­ cal model (Fig. 1), and the researcher adhered closely to this framework throughout the study. The qualitative research process is flexible. In qualitative research, the problem under investigation is addressed from a holis­ tic perspective [39]. For these reasons, the qualitative research method was chosen in the present study. Selection of participants In qualitative research, since it is aimed at examining the people or situations that are the subject of the research in depth rather than generalizing the research results to the population, the purposeful random sampling technique is preferred more [40]. In this study, convenience sampling, one of the purposeful sampling techniques, was used in accordance with the nature of qualitative research and the purpose of the study. Individuals with cardiovascu­ lar disease were included in this study because it is the leading cause of death in Turkey, and the disease group constitutes a large segment of society. The study sample consisted of patients recommended for inpatient treat­ ment following outpatient clinic examinations, who were approached during hospitalization to inquire about their willingness to participate in the study, with those who agreed included in the sample group. Three dif­ ferent types of interviews are mentioned in the literature [35, 43, 44]: structured, semi-structured, and unstruc­ tured interviews. The study preferred the semi-structured interview method because qualitative research is carried out for a specific purpose, requiring adherence to the research problem. With this method, more systematic and comparable information can be obtained from different individuals. Preparation of interview questions The first version of the interview questions created by the researcher was prepared as a draft within the frame­ work of the themes in the model in the thesis study. The draft form was shared with four academics in the field of health management. Changes were made based on the opinions and suggestions of the academics, resulting in the development of a new interview form. The new form was evaluated with the supervisor, thereby finalizing the interview form. The interview form consists of five stages and five ques­ tions. The stages include: i - expectations from the health establishment, ii - expectations from doctors, iii - expec­ tations from nurses, iv - expectations from the treatment and care process, and v - questions to obtain participant demographic information. Although the interview questions were prepared based on the themes in the model and through a certain pro­ cess, additional questions were asked during the inter­ view in order to better understand the research topic and obtain in-depth information. The order of the questions was adjusted based on the participants' responses. Rather than using a rigid list of predefined questions, the interviews were guided by the main research ques­ tion and four sub-research questions derived from the theoretical model. These questions were used as thematic anchors during the interviews. Given the researchers' familiarity with the model struc­ ture, additional follow-up and probing questions were flexibly introduced to explore other relevant dimensions of patient expectations as they emerged during the inter­ views. This approach allowed participants to elaborate on their experiences in their own words while ensuring con­ sistency with the conceptual framework. Validity and reliability Validity and reliability are the most common criteria used to assess the credibility of study results [42]. In qualitative research, validity refers to representing the phenomenon under investigation as it is and in its real­ ity, observing it as unbiasedly as possible, maintaining the integrity of the results, and ensuring the accuracy of the connection between the construct and the data [45, 46]. In this study, theoretical validity (internal validity) was utilized to demonstrate validity. Theoretical valid­ ity is an abstract approach, referring to adhering to the method used for interpreting data when combining the information [47]. This study used a research model devel­ oped based on conceptual and theoretical phenomena, and researcher bias was tried to be prevented by adhering to the model in the collection and application of data. All in all, the findings of the study show that the results are in line with the theoretical and conceptual framework. Reli­ ability refers to the consistency and reproducibility of the collection, interpretation, or analysis of study data [42]. For this reason, the concepts of credibility or consistency are used instead of reliability in qualitative research. One of the methods that can be used for credibility is trian­ gulation. The aim of triangulation is to use the source of information to support each major conclusion. Triangu­ lation can be done in four ways: data source triangula­ tion (using various data sources in the study), investigator triangulation (involving multiple researchers in data col­ lection, analysis, and interpretation), theory triangula­ tion (providing different approaches by reviewing the literature), and method triangulation (collecting abun­ dant data) [48]. In this study, investigator triangulation and theory triangulation were utilized to ensure research credibility or consistency. Data analysis To test the model, themes and categories guiding the research were used in the collection and analysis of quali­ tative data. These themes and categories not only keep the research within a certain focus and boundary but also facilitate the collection and analysis of data. They also guide the researcher in the interpretation of the data. The study utilized the content analysis method. Hsieh & Shannon [49] distinguish three approaches to qualitative content analysis: conventional, summative, and directed. The study used the "directed qualitative content analysis" [49] technique. In other words, the study data were ana­ lyzed not inductively from codes to themes, but deduc­ tively from themes to codes. The audio recordings obtained through the interviews were transcribed after each interview, and the text was read several times to establish a connection with the research question. The codes were created by matching the themes in the model formed as a result of conceptual and theoretical reviews with the statements in the texts obtained through the interviews. Although there was a general consistency between the analysis results obtained through matching and the model, some different catego­ ries emerged as well. The coding process was conducted independently by the researcher and an academic who agreed to do the coding. After the independent coding process was completed, the two studies were compared to determine whether different themes were identified. Once it was established that the two studies were consis­ tent, the coding process for the themes was concluded. After that, qualitative data were analyzed via the NVIVO qualitative data analysis program. To counter criticisms suggesting that interpretations made by researchers lack scientific background in qualitative studies, interpreta­ tions were supported by statistical tables and diagrams to the extent permitted by the software. A coding frame­ work was developed based on the predefined themes, and exemplar quotations were mapped to each cate­ gory to ensure analytical transparency. After the coding and analysis process was completed, findings were not returned to participants for member checking due to patients' clinical conditions and the inpatient setting.

chunk_text: This section presents the findings from the in-depth interviews conducted to answer the research questions, "What are the expectations of patients with cardio­ vascular disease from healthcare services?" and "From whom do patients have these expectations?". The patients' expectations from healthcare services, identi­ fied through interviews, encompassed 7 themes and 23 categories (Table 2). According to the table, the themes, based on their prevalence, are "Access to Service", "Com­ munication", "Information", "Support", "Maintaining Page 6 of 18 Durmuş and Akbolat BMC Health Services Research (2026) 26:279 Patient Dignity", "Hospitality Services", and "Expectations from Treatment Outcome", respectively. The categories under the access to service theme are competence, treat­ ment follow-up, service utilization, procedures, access barrier, and coordination/consultation, those under the communication theme are doctor-patient communica­ tion, nurse-patient communication, and other healthcare professionals-patient communication, those under the information theme are information before treatment, information during treatment, and information after treatment, those under the support theme are emotional support and physical support, those under the main­ taining patient dignity theme are medical care, patient autonomy, and privacy, those under the hospitality ser­ vices theme are comfort, safety, and cleanliness, and those under the expectations from treatment outcome theme are physical well-being, emotional well-being, and social well-being. The answer to the question "What are the expecta­ tions of people with cardiovascular disease from healthcare services?" is contained in the themes and cat­ egories obtained from the interviews. The quoted state­ ments related to the themes and categories are shown in quotation marks in the table in Annex-1. The patient's interview code appears after the quote. The qualitative findings presented below are grounded in verbatim quo­ tations obtained from the interviews. To avoid repetition within the main text, representative participant quota­ tions corresponding to each theme and category are provided in Annex-1, with participant codes indicated. To enhance transparency and credibility, representative verbatim quotations for each category are provided in Annex-1 and are referenced throughout the Results sec­ tion using participant codes. These quotations form the empirical basis of the interpretations reported in the Results section. In this context, the themes and catego­ ries are evaluated and interpreted respectively below. Theme 2: Communication The communication theme reveals patients' expectations regarding the exchange of information with healthcare professionals about their health status, diagnosis, and treatment processes. This theme consists of three cat­ egories addressing the communication expectations of patients with doctors, nurses, and other healthcare pro­ fessionals. In this theme, patients expressed their desire for healthcare professionals to be friendly, respectful, and approachable, to communicate clearly and understand­ ably, to listen attentively to their problems, and to engage in conversation with them. Representative participant quotations supporting these categories are provided in Annex-1. Doctor-patient communication: "Patients emphasized clear, respectful, and empathetic communication with physicians (e.g., G1, G2, G12, G19; see Annex-1)." Nurse-patient communication: "Warm, patient, and reassuring communication by nurses was highlighted (e.g., G10, G14, G16, G18; see Annex-1)." Other healthcare professionals-patient communica­ tion: "Respectful and informative communication with non-clinical staff during admission and coordination was expected (e.g., G2, G3, G4; see Annex-1)." Doctor-Patient communication Patients expect their doctors to listen to them efficiently, engage in open and mutual communication, provide effective explanations during diagnosis and treatment, show respect, exhibit positive behaviors such as courtesy and a smiling demeanor, offer reassurance, and dem­ onstrate sensitivity in their approach. On the contrary, they do not expect them to speak rudely, adopt a conde­ scending and indifferent attitude, or try to dismiss them abruptly. Nurse-Patient communication Patients expect nurses to communicate effectively, engage in conversation during procedures, listen attentively, and speak calmly. They also expect nurses to exhibit positive behaviors such as being smiling, friendly, sympathetic, optimistic, gentle, kind, respectful, and patient. How­ ever, they do not expect nurses to be grim-faced, behave rudely, huff and puff, or bite head off. Other healthcare Professionals-Patient communication The term "other healthcare professionals" refers to pro­ fessionals, aside from doctors and nurses, who typically interact with patients during the management phase of healthcare services. In this category, patients expect other healthcare professionals to communicate with understanding, respect, friendliness, and politeness. Theme 3: Information Patients state that healthcare professionals should inform them or their relatives about the diagnosis of the disease, the operation or treatment process, and its aftermath. The information theme consists of three categories: information before treatment, information during treat­ ment, and information after treatment. Verbatim quotations illustrating these categories are presented in Annex-1. Information before treatment: "Clear and proactive explanations regarding diagnosis and treatment options were expected (e.g., G12, G18; see Annex-1)." Information during treatment: "Ongoing infor­ mation about procedures, medications, and care Page 8 of 18 Durmuş and Akbolat BMC Health Services Research (2026) 26:279 without prompting was emphasized (e.g., G1, G2, G6; see Annex-1)." Information after treatment: "Guidance on post-dis­ charge lifestyle, medication use, and recovery was high­ lighted (e.g., G1, G11; see Annex-1)." Information before treatment Patients expect to receive clear and understandable information about their diagnosis, the status of their dis­ ease, and how they can benefit from healthcare services. Patients also desire to receive information about their illness proactively, rather than having to ask questions, and they seek to know the potential risks associated with receiving or not receiving treatment. They prefer to receive recommendations in this regard and have their relatives informed. Information during treatment This category includes the expectation that patients receive information about the procedures conducted throughout the treatment process, starting from their admission to the clinical ward. Patients expect to receive clear and comprehensive information about planned care, treatment, and all procedures to be performed, without having to ask questions and in a manner that they can easily comprehend. In other words, every stage of the treatment should be explained to the patient in detail by the healthcare professional. Patients also want to know when they will be discharged from the health establishment, and they expect their companions to be informed about the procedures. Information after treatment Patients expect to be informed about what they need to do to regain their quality of life after discharge. They want to know what exercises to do, what to eat, and what to avoid, and they expect to be guided to regain their health. Theme 4: support This theme encompasses healthcare professionals assist­ ing patients or their relatives during their time at the health establishment. Here, support means meeting all the emotional and physical needs of patients without being demanded. This support should be provided by healthcare professionals without questioning. The theme consists of two categories: physical and emotional. Supporting participant statements for each category are summarized in Annex-1. chunk_text: Theme 1: Access to service Based on the interview findings, the most important theme was found to be "access to service". Access is addressed in terms of the availability of necessary ser­ vices as well as how services are provided at the point of care [50]. Access to service involves both the availability of needed healthcare services and the treatment to be received [51]. The theme consists of six categories: com­ petence, treatment follow-up, service utilization, proce­ dures, access barrier, and coordination/consultation. As to competence, patients expect healthcare profes­ sionals to be competent and proficient in their tasks and procedures. The literature contains similar studies. For example, Aoun et al. [52] found that patients prioritize the doctor's role as a medical expert and put it at the top of the list of competences. In their study, 56.8% of the patients prioritized the clinical competence and exper­ tise of the physician. The second most prioritized compe­ tency in that study was professionalism. In Amarat's [53] thesis, aimed at determining the antecedents of hospital reputation based on patients (clinic and polyclinic) and potential patients, the competence of doctors and other professionals received the greatest emphasis. Also, medi­ cal expertise (competence) is at the center of the Can­ MEDS (The Canadian Medical Education Directives for Specialist) framework, and all other competence frame­ works agree that a good doctor should excel in ques­ tioning, examining, diagnosing, and treating the patient [54-56]. Treatment follow-up, where the patient's follow-up and treatment procedures are carried out, is one of the subdimensions of patients' expectations regarding access to service. In some studies on treatment follow-up in the literature, it is stated that individuals expect to be fol­ lowed up by nurses [57], their condition to be monitored, nurses to make efforts to meet their needs after discharge from the hospital [58], the doctor to continuously moni­ tor their condition and schedule the next appointment for further treatment [59, 60], and the doctor to make a phone call within 24-48 h [61]. The service utilization category pertains to patients' uti­ lization of services provided by the health establishment and healthcare professionals according to their needs, as well as their desire to have those needs met. Bowling et al. [9] report that patients expect timely appointments with doctors, minimal waiting times, avoidance of delays, access to a specific doctor, appropriate medical tests, accurate diagnoses, consultations to be timely or of suffi­ cient duration, and favorable outcomes. In the literature, it is also noted that patients expect nurses to be accessi­ ble when needed [62], to respond promptly to their calls [57, 58], doctors to allocate sufficient time, ease of sched­ uling appointments with doctors, and no limitations on working hours [63, 64]. The procedures category is about patients' expecta­ tions regarding the process of procedures performed in the health establishment. Tekin [65] determined that the majority of patients applying to health establishments were uncomfortable with bureaucratic procedures and waiting in queues. Theme 2: Communication Communication is the second important theme that emerged from the findings. This theme focuses on what patients expect from their interactions with all health­ care professionals involved in the diagnosis, treatment, and discharge processes. Patients' expectations involve certain attitudes in communication such as healthcare professionals being friendly, respectful, approachable, speaking clearly and understandably, and listening care­ fully to their problems. In this context, the theme is addressed in three categories: doctor-patient communi­ cation, nurse-patient communication, and other health­ care professionals-patient communication. The doctor-patient communication category focuses on how patients expect to interact with the doctor from the moment they encounter them until they leave the health establishment. Patients expect doctors to welcome them with a smile and a handshake, make eye contact with them, treat them with respect, talk, chat, or engage in friendly banter, as well as demonstrate positive body language. Patients expect to be taken seriously by their doctor, but not to be ignored or treated as a person. They also want their doctor not to act indifferent and not to appear unprofessional [81]. Similarly, patients tend to desire to be greeted and known or recognized by their doctor through 'personal' or 'interpersonal' continu­ ity [82, 83]. The literature also suggests that patients expect their doctor to listen carefully [61-63, 84], speak in a clear and understandable language [67, 84], include them in communication [61, 62, 84], be understanding, respectful, polite, friendly, and show courtesy [9, 59, 62, 63, 67, 85]. The nurse-patient communication category addresses patients' expectations for effective communication with nurses and positive behaviors from nurses during the care process. In their national (Turkish) literature review study, Özsoy, Özgür, & Durmaz Akyol [86] found that most of the studies identified patients' expectations of nursing care to include joy, interest, understanding, kind­ ness, and helpfulness. These expectations regarding nurs­ ing care vary between 30% and 98%. In another study, patients' expectations regarding communication, infor­ mation, assistance, and meeting requests within patient admission and treatment were high [87]. It is also noted that patients expect nurses to be friendly, respectful, optimistic, warm, understanding, and attentive, but not harsh and rude [57, 58, 88-91]. Theme 3: Information Patients are curious about and need to be informed of the type of treatment they will receive for their condition, the potential effects of the treatment, how the care services will be provided, and what the possible side effects of the recommended medications will be during the post-treat­ ment recovery process. In this context, it is crucial to offer information that aligns with the expectations of the patient or their relatives. According to studies in the liter­ ature, patients expect both themselves and their relatives to be informed clearly and comprehensively, in simple language, by doctors, nurses, and other healthcare pro­ fessionals about their health condition, the procedures undertaken or to be undertaken, their risks and benefits, the causes of their health problem, how to manage them, the tests, surgeries, medications, and treatments during treatment, as well as the medications, equipment, and exercises they will have after discharge [9, 57-59, 61, 62, 66, 67, 84, 96, 97]. For this reason, healthcare professionals should empathize and sympathize with patients and encourage them against their concerns [98]. Research reports that patients expect physical and emotional support [99], spiritual support and help [97], hope and support [61], support for care [62], physical support [100], and support and reassurance [101]. As a result of the study, there is compatibility between this model and the literature-based model of patients' expectations regard­ ing health and healthcare services. The themes related to patient expectations are consistent in both models, but there are differences in some categories. The cost cat­ egory, which is included in the theme of access to service in the model in the thesis study, is not among the catego­ ries obtained in the study. This could be attributed to the fact that individuals receive healthcare services covered by general health insurance (GHI). The number of indi­ viduals covered by GHI in Turkey has been increasing over the years. According to the 2009 data from Turkey's Social Security Institution, there were 58.591.604 individ­ uals covered by social insurance back then. That number is insurance designed primarily to safeguard individuals' health and cover their expenses in the event of healthrelated risks. It ensures that all members of society ben­ efit from healthcare services in an equal, accessible, and effective manner against disease risks that may arise, regardless of the economic power and willingness of the individuals covered by the insurance. This allows indi­ viduals to receive healthcare services within the scope of insurance. The categories not included in the model in the thesis study but obtained in the study are social well-being and other healthcare professionals-patient communica­ tion. The social well-being category is under the theme of expectations from treatment outcome, while other healthcare professionals-patient communication is under the theme of communication. Patients with social wellbeing expectation expect to regain their quality of life as soon as possible after treatment, enabling them to estab­ lish social relationships and continue their lives not as patients but as healthy individuals recognized by society. Another difference between the model derived in the present study and the model in the thesis study Fig. 2 Empirically derived model of cardiovascular patients' expectations based on qualitative findings Page 14 of 18 Durmuş and Akbolat BMC Health Services Research (2026) 26:279 pertains to from whom patients expect healthcare ser­ vices. Accordingly, the communication theme was incor­ porated into patients' expectations from the healthcare organization, in addition to the model found in the litera­ ture. The reason for this is the desire of patients to engage in communication with other healthcare profession­ als upon arriving at the health establishment. Another addition is related to patients' expectations from nurses. Differently from the model in the thesis study, patients expect nurses to support them. Patients expect to receive emotional support because they cannot cope with emo­ tional problems such as fear and sadness and feel helpless during the service delivery process. Although the overall structure of the empirical model resembles the literature-based framework, Fig. 2 reflects data-driven modifications based on patients' narratives, thereby representing the contextualized expectations of cardiovascular patients in the present study. The characteristics of the study population are largely comparable to those reported in previous qualitative studies examining patient expectations in hospitalbased cardiovascular care. Similar to earlier research, the participants in this study were predominantly mid­ dle-aged and older adults with chronic cardiovascular conditions and multiple comorbidities, receiving inpa­ tient treatment. Therefore, while the findings should be interpreted within the context of a single-center and pandemicperiod setting, the expectation patterns identified in this study align with those observed in comparable patient populations in the literature. This supports the relevance and contextual validity of the findings, particularly for inpatient cardiology services. This is because patients' expectations from healthcare ser­ vices significantly impact receiving treatment, the care process, and the outcome. Accordingly, patients expect their medical procedures to be carried out quickly and healthcare professionals to show a reassuring approach from the moment they apply to the health establish­ ment. They seek patient-centered communication, clear information, and emotional support from health­ care professionals during the treatment and care pro­ cess. They emphasize the importance of competent doctors and nurses performing medical procedures with care in a comfortable and relaxed environ­ ment, highlighting the need for follow-up treatment and check-ups as well. As a result of treatment, they expect their physical and emotional well-being to be maintained or strengthened and their quality of life to improve. All in all, these expectations reflect the way patients think and show how seemingly small things can actually have a significant impact on patients. Conducting the study in a single cardiology clinic dur­ ing the COVID-19 pandemic may have influenced patients' expectations, particularly in relation to safety concerns, emotional support needs, and access to ser­ vices. Pandemic-related restrictions, fear of infection, and changes in hospital routines could have shaped patients' perceptions and priorities during hospital­ ization. Therefore, the findings should be interpreted within the context of the pandemic period. In addition, the single-center design and the inclu­ sion of only hospitalized cardiovascular patients may limit the transferability of the findings to other clini­ cal settings or patient groups. BRAIN offers a teachable template to support clinician training and future validation studies (e.g., expert consensus and real-world implementation pilots), with the potential to optimize functional, patient-centered outcomes. Background/Objectives: Clinical reasoning is essential in neurological rehabilitation, in which patient management is complex and multifactorial. However, existing models lack operationalization for neurophysiotherapy practice. This paper proposes the Biopsychosocial Reasoning Approach In Neurophysiotherapy (BRAIN) framework, a unified clinical reasoning model that integrates the International Classification of Functioning, Disability, and Health (ICF) with neurophysiotherapy-specific domains of physical function. Methods: The BRAIN framework was developed by integrating previously validated models: the ICF, the American Physical Therapy Association (APTA) patient-management process, and Kisner and Colby’s interrelated aspects of physical function, adapted for neurological populations. The model employs a biopsychosocial, patient-centered, and goal-oriented approach, thereby providing a structured workflow for examination, evaluation, diagnosis, prognosis, intervention, and outcomes assessment. Results: The BRAIN framework provides an operationalized mapping between ICF body functions and neurophysiotherapy-specific impairment domains, a clear separation between body functions and body structures, tiered assessment pathways addressing patient heterogeneity, and a unified language for interdisciplinary communication. The model incorporates shared decision-making and goal-oriented reasoning within the clinical workflow. Conclusions: The BRAIN framework offers a structured, teachable template for clinical reasoning in neurological physiotherapy. As a theoretical proposal, there is a need for empirical validation through expert consensus and clinical implementation studies.

chunk_text: Clinical reasoning is often regarded as the foundation of clinical practice [1]. As posited by several authors, the construct is best characterized as multidimensional, a perspective that underscores its inherent complexity and integration of disparate domains [2]. It is regarded as a fundamental skillset for healthcare professionals and has been the focus of extensive research by various healthcare professionals [2,3]. Its definition is subject to variation based on the discipline: it is more focused on diagnosis when adopted by physicians or on the decision-making process when used by psychologists, physiotherapists or occupational therapists [4]. However, clinical reasoning can be defined as "the mental process that happens when a healthcare professional encounters a patient and is expected to draw a conclusion about (a) the nature and possible causes of complaints or abnormal conditions of the patient, (b) a likely diagnosis, and (c) patient management actions to be taken" [5]. The clinical reasoning process comprises a multitude of interacting factors, including the patient, the clinician, and the clinical environment. The prevailing categorization of this phenomenon encompasses two primary types: inductive (or forward) reasoning and deductive (or backwards) reasoning [6,7]. Inductive reasoning comprises two subsystems: the first relies on pattern recognition, predominantly driven by the clinician's expertise and experiential knowledge; the second involves a slower, more effortful analytical thinking process [8]. These two systems are situated on a cognitive continuum, ranging from immediate, intuitive recognition to deliberate and prolonged analytical reasoning [8,9]. Conversely, deductive clinical reasoning involves constructing a mental model, or a set of models, derived from general knowledge, established theoretical principles, and clinical guidelines. The use of these models is predicated on their capacity to facilitate the formulation of hypotheses concerning the patient's presentation and possible outcomes. Clinicians then systematically evaluate these hypotheses by collecting and analyzing evidence to confirm or refute them. In the absence of disconfirming evidence during clinical assessment, initial mental models are reinforced, thereby supporting valid clinical conclusions and facilitating sound clinical decision-making [10]. Clinical reasoning is an essential competency for physiotherapists. It must be an ongoing process that evolves along the continuum of the patient's rehabilitation. Furthermore, it must be carried out in a multidisciplinary manner, integrating cognitive, psychomotor and affective skills [4,11]. In the domain of neurologic physiotherapy, we can observe an evolution in the decision-making process. The initial theories, grounded in neurophysiological perspectives, aimed to achieve better rehabilitation outcomes based on Brain Sci. 2026, 16, 235 3 of 21 personal experiences [12], and subsequently, a more scientific approach emerged within the biopsychosocial model, encompassing a more rigorous and systematic framework [13,14]. Furthermore, empirical evidence suggests that practicing clinicians, including physiotherapists, often rely heavily on implicit, experience-based heuristics rather than explicit theoretical frameworks [18]. Clinical decision-making in real-world settings is often influenced by personal experience accumulated over years of practice, guidance from mentors and supervisors, and local workplace culture or protocols [18]. While such experiential reasoning can be efficient and contextually appropriate, its reliance on tacit knowledge poses challenges for standardization, education, interdisciplinary communication, and quality assurance [19]. In the domain of neurological rehabilitation, challenges such as patient heterogeneity, complexity, and the need for a multidisciplinary collaboration underscore the importance of a shared, explicit reasoning language [20]. Thus, there is an urgent need for structured frameworks that can link theoretical models with clinical practice-frameworks that are both evidence-based and operationally feasible for real-world implementation [21]. The primary objective of this study was to present an updated and operational model of clinical reasoning specific to neurological physiotherapy, which facilitates decision-making, improves interdisciplinary communication, and optimizes patients' functional outcomes. 2. Foundations and Development of Clinical Reasoning Models in Physiotherapy In 1970, Brunnstrom published her seminal work "Movement Therapy in Hemiplegia: A Neurophysiological Approach", basing her hypotheses on experiments carried out on animals at the beginning of the 20th century [22]. These studies provide the fundamental bases for recovery after brain damage. In this context, authors such as Sherrington began to observe the phenotypes of spasticity based on the location and severity of the lesion [23-25]. Brunnstrom's method is predicated on post-stroke synergies that represent primitive reflexes liberated from higher control, thereby suggesting developmental regression [22,26]. She emphasizes the pivotal role of spasticity in the context of paresis, asserting that its elimination should be prioritized as a fundamental step in addressing the condition-a contested position [22]. Research shows limited and debated evidence for physiotherapy's impact on spasticity [27-29]. NDT emerged from this perspective, notably the Bobath concept, defined as a problem-solving framework for assessing and treating function, movement, and tone impairments from central nervous system lesions using key handling points and reflex patterns [30,31]. This approach is characterized as complex, multidimensional, and individualized, emphasizing "how" tasks are performed while avoiding compensatory movements [32]. The clinical reasoning behind the Bobath concept is based on neurophysiological grounds that aim to achieve 'normal movement' in individuals with brain damage through the facilitation of movement to enhance motor learning [33]. In 2001, the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) was approved by the World Health Organization (WHO), following a global collaboration that provided a comprehensive conceptualization of disability [40,41]. First, the health status of the patient is determined, which refers to the diseases or disorders that affect the patient. Secondly, the concept of "body functions and structures" is introduced. The term "body functions" is defined as the physiological processes of body systems, which also encompasses psychological functions. In contrast, "body structures" refer to the anatomical components of the body, including organs and limbs, along with their respective components. Third, activity is defined as the ability to complete an action or task. This methodology is operationalized through SMART objectives, which stipulate that therapeutic goals must be Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic, and Time-bound [47]. The development of the Goal Attainment Scale (GAS) was motivated by the necessity to quantify these objectives and to facilitate the translation of this methodology into research settings. [48]. GAS employs a 5-point Likert scale to evaluate the extent of goal attainment. A score of 0 indicates the expected outcome following intervention, scores of +1 and +2 denote outcomes that are greater and much greater than expected, respectively, whereas scores of −1 and −2 indicate outcomes that are less and much less than expected [49]. chunk_text: In conclusion, the present study proposes a comprehensive framework for clinical reasoning in neurological physiotherapy. This framework integrates the Kisner and Colby interrelated aspects of physical function within the classical APTA proposal and the ICF framework to create a more adaptable and patient-centered approach. The BRAIN framework is predicated on the biopsychosocial model and goal-oriented strategies. These elements empower physiotherapists to address the unique challenges of managing neurological patients, with a focus on enhancing patient participation and quality of life. The unified model under consideration encourages effective interdisciplinary collaboration and offers a clear pathway for improving rehabilitation outcomes, thereby addressing a gap in current clinical practice. title: Assessing the Accuracy of Symptoms and Adverse Events Reporting for Lung Cancer Treatment in the Danish National Patient Registry
keywords: Danish national patient registry, systemic anti-cancer therapies, oncology, clinical manifestations, information extraction, journal notes
chunk_text: Systemic anti-cancer and radiation therapies for lung cancer often cause adverse events that impair quality of life. Therefore, it may be counterproductive if patient survival is too short for any benefit. Decision support tools predicting short-term mortality in patients with lung cancer have been investigated using data from the Danish National Patient Registry (DNPR). However, the extent of the DNPR’s information on clinical manifestations of anti-cancer treatments, particularly in lung cancer, remains unknown. We assessed the validity of clinical manifestation reporting in the DNPR to evaluate its usability in decision support tools and epidemiological studies. Ninety-five patients treated for lung cancer at the Department of Oncology, Aalborg University Hospital, who died between 2015 and 2022 were randomly selected. Four raters independently extracted clinical manifestations from patients’ journals. Interrater agreement was measured using Light’s kappa (threshold ≥ 0.41). Extracted manifestations were matched to DNPR data, and concordance was quantified using the F1-score, aggregating by date, week, month, quarter, year, and patient. Interrater agreement ranged from moderate to perfect, except for constipation. Concordance between journal and DNPR data was low for most clinical manifestations. F1-scores for dyspnea, hemoptysis, and pain, almost exclusively at the patient level, suggested moderate reporting in the DNPR. Concordance between the DNPR and patient journals was limited for minor and moderate clinical manifestations, but severe manifestations, such as dyspnea, hemoptysis, and pain, showed moderate agreement, showcasing some usability in this limited context. This study also demonstrates the availability of rich data about clinical manifestations in journal notes. Despite potential biases in these data, this study highlights the potential in the extraction of clinical manifestations directly from patient journals, notably using Natural Language Processing, to obtain more detailed data for epidemiological studies or to build machine learning-based decision support tools.

The raters were undergraduate students in Medicine and Medicine with Industrial Specialization at Aalborg University. The rating was performed under the supervision of an experienced oncologist at Aalborg University Hospital. The extracted data, referred to as journal data, consisted of patient ID, predefined category, the exact wording of how the category was described, grading, and date of occurrence. The exact wording was used to assign the entry to one of the eleven categories of symptoms and adverse events, hereafter referred to as clinical manifestations, which were selected based on their relevance and frequency in a randomly selected subset of 12 patient journals from the study population. Twelve journals were selected to ensure equal distribution among the four raters and to maintain a sample size above ten journals, which was considered sufficient to identify common clinical manifestations in the patient journals. The 11 clinical manifestations included constipation, coughing, diarrhea, dyspnea, fatigue, hemoptysis, headache, hoarseness, nausea, pain, and weight loss. The grading was performed according to international guidelines of the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE)11 with the purpose of standardizing the collection of data. Analysis Interrater Agreement Analysis Interrater agreement was evaluated between the four raters using Light's kappa.13 To evaluate this, data entries from two raters at a time were matched based on the patient ID, clinical manifestation, and date. In cases where multiple assessments by the same rater for the same clinical manifestation were performed on the same day, only the assessment with the highest grading was retained. If a rater did not report any assessment on a day for a clinical manifestation, while other raters did, a value of −1 was used as grading for this rater. Confidence intervals for Light's kappa were calculated by bootstrapping by resampling with replacement of the identified occurrences and their corresponding six possible dependent pairwise assessments 1000 times. Light's kappa is an extension of Cohen's kappa for scenarios involving more than two raters. Therefore, a standardized interpretation of kappa values was used to evaluate the results.14 Light's kappa was interpreted as follows: Light's kappa 0.61-0.80 substantial agreement, 0.81-1.00 almost perfect agreement, and 1.00 perfect agreement.14,15 This interpretation allows for Light's kappa > 0.41 to be considered acceptable. Danish National Patient Registry Compared to Patient Journals For entries manually extracted from the four patients shared across raters, a consensus among raters was used. This consensus was obtained by comparing journal ratings and grading of clinical manifestations based on the majority of equal gradings. The journals reviewed by only one rater were deemed accurate upon achieving an acceptable level of interrater agreement. To evaluate the concordance between the DNPR and journal data, records from both datasets were generated, consisting of patient ID, clinical manifestation, and date. For each patient and clinical manifestation, at most one record per date was kept in both datasets, hereafter referred to as an occurrence. Six time period aggregations were considered: aggregating on date (no aggregation), week, month, quarter, year, and patient (no temporal criteria) and keeping only one record per aggregated time period. chunk_text: Main Results This study compared data extracted from patient journals and the DNPR to evaluate how accurately the DNPR reflect clinical manifestations in lung cancer patients. The high interrater agreement for most symptoms indicates that the manual journal data extraction was generally reliable, although the lower agreement for constipation (kappa = 0.46) suggest that some clinical manifestations are more prone to subjective interpretation. The concordance between the journal data and the DNPR was consistently low across all time intervals, highlighting the limitations of the DNPR, as an administrative tool, for clinical manifestation reporting. At the patient level, only severe clinical manifestations, such as dyspnea, hemoptysis, and pain reached an F1-score >0.25, with only dyspnea reaching >0.5, suggesting a moderate level of reporting of these clinical manifestations at the patient level in the DNPR. This pattern that the DNPR primarily reflects clinical manifestations that are clinically significant and likely to influence treatment decisions or resource use, while minor or moderate clinical manifestations stay underreported. Strength and Limitations This population-based study analyzed a randomly selected population of patients with lung cancer at the Department of Oncology in the NDR. Random selection limits selection bias.17 However, including patients from only one region could lead to a lack of generalizability of the results to Denmark and the rest of Scandinavia.10 Clinical Manifestations No. of Patients (%) No. of Occurrences (per Affected Patients) Fatigue 94 (99) 585 (6.2) Hemoptysis 64 (67) 133 (2.1) Headache 60 (63) 200 (3.3) Hoarseness 49 (52) 83 (1.7) Nausea 77 (81) 349 (4.5) Pain 93 (98) 1169 (12.6) Weight loss 92 (97) 459 (5.0) Notes: The number of patients corresponds to the patients having at least one record. We decided to include patients based, not on their diagnosis date, but on their death date. The rationale was to have a complete picture of each patient trajectory, from diagnosis to death. This design choice could be seen as conditioning on future events but death being an ineluctable outcome for all patients, we considered it as acceptable since there was a limited patient selection on diagnosis date. Indeed, thanks to the long available history, having access to all patient data from 1991, we ensured a limited selection bias based on survival, allowing us to include patients with diverse survival coughing, weight loss, nausea, headache, diarrhea, constipation, hemoptysis, and hoarseness. The choice to scrutinize 12 patient journals to identify clinical manifestations can be considered arbitrary. Indeed, this was not based on a proper power calculation before the study, as it was intended to be exploratory. The assessments from these journals could possibly be biased owing to more thorough examinations compared with the remaining patients. A limitation of this study could also be seen in the reliability of the reference standard. In this study, manually extracted patient journal data were considered the ground truth, leading to methodological challenges. First, the raters professional background may have influenced data quality. Although supervised by an oncologist, students may be more prone to misinterpret clinical notes and the severity of the clinical manifestations, which could be the cause of the low interrater agreement for constipation (Light's kappa = 0.46). Second, the clinical manifestations reported by the patients were selectively recorded by clinicians, depending on their clinical relevance and significance. Thus, the patient journals themselves can be inherently incomplete and non-standardized leading to documentation bias. Third, the two data sources use different systems for describing clinical manifestations. The gradings based of CTCAE shows how severe the clinical manifestation is, while the DNPR codes only tell us if the clinical manifestation is present or not. In this study, any CTCAE grade above 0 was treated as equal to a DNPR entry, but this may be seen as an oversimplification. Interrater Agreement Interrater agreement analysis was conducted using Light's kappa to assess the similarity of ratings by the raters across 11 clinical manifestations in the patient journals of the four patients. The interrater agreement varies among clinical manifestations, as shown in Figure 1. This variation could be attributed to several factors. First, some clinical manifestations are more difficult to grade because of an insufficient level of detail in patient journals. Second, the total number of clinical manifestations extracted varied among raters. Human error, either by overlooking a clinical manifestation or documenting one that is not present, may account for missing or added value. Therefore, Light's kappa was calculated without accounting for the different numbers of clinical manifestations noted by each rater. When employing Light's kappa, an extension of Cohen's kappa, it is expected that the data will be on a nominal scale.18

Human error, either by overlooking a clinical manifestation or documenting one that is not present, may account for missing or added value. Therefore, Light's kappa was calculated without accounting for the different numbers of clinical manifestations noted by each rater. When employing Light's kappa, an extension of Cohen's kappa, it is expected that the data will be on a nominal scale.18 However, only a few gradings adhered to this scale, while the majority were on an ordinal scale. In addition, the standardized interpretation of kappa values is criticized when used in health-related studies because it allows for a kappa of 0.41 to be acceptable.14 Therefore, it is suggested that a kappa value ≥0.60 is the acceptable standard in health-related studies.14 Thus, the only clinical manifestation with an unacceptable agreement was constipation (Light's kappa = 0.46). These findings indicate that the manually extracted data from patient journals are reliable. However, as the mean Light's kappa value for constipation is under the acceptable standard in health-related studies, manually extracted data on this cannot necessarily be considered the truth. Concordance Between Patient Journals and the Danish National Patient Registry This study explored whether the DNPR could serve as a source for clinical manifestations for decision support tools and future research. While the DNPR did not reflect the full spectrum of clinical manifestations documented in patient journals, it did reflect, in some cases, severe and clinically significant manifestations, such as dyspnea, hemoptysis, and pain. Dyspnea and pain were the most frequently reported and showed the highest concordance with journal data. These findings align with a study by Chowienczyk et al who identified dyspnea and cough as common presenting symptoms in lung cancer patients from 2000 to 2017.19 Although coughing was documented in most patient journals, its low F1-score indicates that it is less consistently recorded in the DNPR. In addition, Chowienczyk et al found that the presence of chest pain is dynamic and decreases over time.19 However, the current study generally considered pain beyond the chest pain. It is important to interpret these findings in the light if the DNPR's primary purpose. title: Turkish version of the Nurse Intuition Patient Deterioration Scale: cross-cultural adaptation and validation study
keywords: Scale adaptation, Psychometric evaluation, Validity and reliability, Intuition, Medical-surgical nursing, Deterioration
chunk_text: This study aimed to adapt the Nurse Intuition Patient Deterioration Scale into Turkish and to evaluate its validity and reliability among nurses working in medical-surgical wards. Unrecognized clinical deterioration is a critical patient safety issue in hospital settings. Although structured monitoring tools such as the National Early Warning Score are widely used, they do not fully capture the complexity of bedside assessments. Nurses’ intuition—the ability to rapidly recognize deterioration—plays an indispensable role in early detection. This was a methodological study focusing on evaluating the measurement properties of the scale, including its reliability and validity. The translation and cultural adaptation process followed the stages of forward translation, synthesis, back translation, expert committee review, and pretesting. For 98 patients, a total of 776 patient assessments were conducted by 40 nurses in this study. The overall scale-level content validity ratio (average) was 0.822, indicating strong overall expert consensus and satisfactory content validity. The overall Cronbach’s alpha coefficient for the scale was 0.797, suggesting good internal consistency. For criterion validity, the relationship between the Nurse Intuition Patient Deterioration Scale scores and the National Early Warning Score-2 was examined; higher Nurse Intuition Patient Deterioration Scale scores were associated with higher National Early Warning Score-2 scores. The Turkish version of the Nurse Intuition Patient Deterioration Scale demonstrated strong psychometric properties, confirming its reliability, construct validity, and criterion-related validity. This study contributes to the theoretical advancement of nursing science by bridging the gap between intuitive expertise and empirical measurement. In practice, the Nurse Intuition Patient Deterioration Scale can serve as an evidence-based tool to support clinical decision-making. Not applicable. The online version contains

chunk_text: Unrecognized clinical deterioration is a critical patient safety issue in hospital settings. Worldwide, a substan­ tial proportion of in-hospital adverse events-including unplanned transfers to intensive care units (ICUs), car­ diac arrests, and preventable mortality-are attributed to delays in detecting deterioration on general wards [1, 2]. Health professionals need to adopt robust, up-to‐ date skills and competencies in observing and assessing patient deterioration [3]. Early recognition and timely intervention reduce morbidity and mortality, but diagno­ sis remains challenging due to the subtle and nonspecific nature of early warning signs. Hospital-wide early warn­ ing scores (EWS) based on nursing surveillance patterns have been shown to be associated with reduced in-hospi­ tal mortality, length of stay, and sepsis risk [4]. Although structured monitoring tools such as the Modified Early Warning Score (MEWS) and the National Early Warning Score (NEWS) are widely used, they do not fully capture the complexity of bedside assessments [1]. Moreover, state-of-the-art trend-based early warning scores lack clinical observations [5]. On the other hand, in practice, nurses often notice that "something is wrong" before measurable changes occur in physiological parameters, highlighting the importance of intuitive judgment in clin­ ical surveillance [6]. "Nurses' worry" is an important early indicator of clini­ cal deterioration. Intuition-based nursing assessments may be particularly valuable in the early phase, when vital signs have not yet reached thresholds for rapid response team activation [1, 7]. Nurses' intuition-the ability to rapidly recognize deterioration based on experiential knowledge, subtle cues, and holistic patient assessmentsupports early detection and timely escalation of care and may be associated with improved outcomes such as reduced ICU transfers [8-11]. Qualitative and observa­ tional studies have consistently shown that nurses rely on gut feelings, behavioral changes, and nonverbal indica­ tors to predict deterioration, which often precede mea­ surable changes in vital signs [1, 10]. Despite its importance, intuition has historically been undervalued in evidence-based frameworks, partly due to difficulties in operationalizing and measuring this con­ struct. Without standardized tools, intuition risks being dismissed as subjective rather than recognized as a valid component of clinical judgment. To address this gap, Haegdorens and colleagues devel­ oped the Nurse Intuition Patient Deterioration Scale (NIPDS), which quantifies nurses' intuitive recogni­ tion of patient decline [12]. The instrument provides a structured means of capturing intuitive judgments, transforming subjective impressions into measurable data. The NIPDS consists of items reflecting the cogni­ tive, affective, and experiential components of intuition in clinical practice, and responses yield a score indicat­ ing the degree of perceived patient risk. Initial validation studies demonstrated acceptable psychometric proper­ ties, supporting its use in both research and practice as a complementary tool to traditional early warning [12]. To our knowledge, no validated instrument is cur­ rently available in Turkish to assess nurses' intuition spe­ cifically in the context of patient deterioration, although intuition has previously been examined in Turkish nurs­ ing students through a validated scale-highlighting the need for a clinical tool such as the NIPDS for practic­ ing nurses [13, 14]. While Turkish hospitals have widely adopted physiological

Similar crosscultural adaptations of nursing scales in other countries have demonstrated that culturally adapted tools can retain strong psychometric properties, providing a prec­ edent for such work [15]. Furthermore, a Turkish version of the NIPDS could foster greater recognition of intuition in nursing education, clinical protocols, and multidisci­ plinary discussions on patient safety.

chunk_text: This was a methodologic study focusing on evaluating the measurement properties of the scale, including its reli­ ability and validity. The study consisted of two phases. In phase 1, the NIPDS was translated and culturally adapted into Turkish following guidelines [15]. In phase 2, the psychometric properties of the Turkish version of the NIPDS were evaluated through a cross-sectional survey. Reporting standards This study was conducted in accordance with interna­ tionally recognized methodological guidelines for crosscultural adaptation and psychometric evaluation of measurement instruments. The translation and cultural Page 3 of 10 Pamir Aksoy et al. BMC Nursing (2026) 25:212 adaptation processes followed the stages proposed by Beaton et al. [16] which include forward translation, syn­ thesis, back translation, expert committee review, and pretesting. The study was conducted and reported in accordance with the COSMIN standards for evaluating measurement properties [17, 18]. In addition, to ensure methodological rigor and transparent reporting of reliability analyses, the study adhered to the Guidelines for Reporting Reliability and Agreement Studies (GRRAS) [19]. Setting We used a convenience sampling method to recruit eli­ gible patients who were hospitalized in medical-surgical inpatient wards of a tertiary teaching and research hospi­ was conducted during the predefined data collection period, and all patients who met the inclusion criteria and were available during the study period were invited to participate. Four wards were selected by an expert committee comprising the research team and the nurse administrator of the hospital, considering patient char­ acteristics. These wards were purposefully chosen as they care for patients who require continuous inpatient follow-up, enabling nurses to monitor clinical trends and detect early signs of deterioration. Patients requiring pre­ operative and postoperative care, long-term follow-up and treatment, and inpatient treatment of acute illnesses are admitted to these wards. The primary nursing care model is being applied at this facility by two shifts (day and night). Each shift has its own nurse-patient ratio and is planned by the charge nurse according to the nursing staff profile and patient characteristics. Sampling In the application of a scale to another culture, it is rec­ ommended to reach a participant number 5-30 times greater than the number of items in the scale [20, 21]. As the scale, which was to be tested for validity and reli­ ability, contained nine items, the sample size was planned as 45-270 patient assessments. A total of 40 nurses par­ ticipated in the study, and 98 patients were evaluated 776 times using the NIPDS during the data collection period. In addition, the same patient could be assessed by more than one nurse across shifts. Therefore, the dataset con­ tained repeated assessments and potential clustering at both the patient and nurse-level. However, the number of assessments per patient varied, as nurses completed the NIPDS at different time points based on clinical need and patient status. The NIPDS consists of nine items, and our sampling size met this criterion with a ratio of approxi­ mately 86:1, which exceeds the recommended range. However, the number of assessments per patient varied, as nurses completed the NIPDS at different time points based on clinical need and patient status. The NIPDS consists of nine items, and our sampling size met this criterion with a ratio of approxi­ mately 86:1, which exceeds the recommended range. Participants Inclusion criteria for participants were as follows: patients age > 18, verbally confirmed to be assessed by their primary nurse. Exclusion criteria for participant patients were as follows: same-day surgery or outpatient, pregnancy, and having mechanical ventilation support. Inclusion criteria for participant nurses were willing­ ness to participate and actively working as a bedside nurse in the medical-surgical wards during the study period. Nurses with different levels of clinical experience were eligible to participate. Exclusion criteria for partici­ pant nurses were being a nursing student/trainee nurse. Ethical considerations Ward nurses voluntarily participated in this study and were recruited by the principal investigator following approval from the ward charge nurse. The nurses were informed about the possible implications of participa­ tion and their right to withdraw at any time. Individu­ als who participated in the study were informed that their responses would remain confidential and would be used for academic research purposes only. The authors ensured confidentiality throughout the data collection and processing. All NIPDS forms were registered by nurses working on the study wards and nicknamed for data collection. The dataset was pseudonymized before data analysis. The researchers were never in contact with any patients. Measures/instruments Nurse Intuition Patient Deterioration Scale (NIPDS): The NIPDS is a validated tool designed for nurses to assess patient deterioration, comprising nine items: decreased ability to verbally communicate, feeling unwell, altered facial expressions, lethargy, restlessness, behavioral changes, abnormal skin color (pale, red, yellow, or gray), a staring or penetrating gaze, and reduced responsive­ ness. The instrument involves scoring each item on a 3-point Likert scale, ranging from "not present" to "very present." Previous studies have demonstrated its excellent construct validity and internal consistency, as well as its high accuracy in predicting urgent physician assistance, resuscitation team calls, patient death, and unplanned transfers to intensive or medium care [12]. The National Early Warning Score (NEWS-2): The NEWS-2 is a risk assessment tool developed to improve the detection of clinical deterioration in adult patients within acute care environments. It aims to facilitate prompt critical care interventions and enhance patient outcomes [22]. A panel of 10 independent experts reviewed and evaluated each item individually. The clarity and relevance of each item were evaluated by the experts using a three-point rating scale (1: clear/relevant/appropriate, 2: requires modifi­ cation to be appropriate, 3: not clear/relevant/appropri­ ate). The relevance of intuition in nursing has long been emphasized in both theoretical and empirical literature. Benner's novice-to-expert model established that intui­ tive judgment develops as a hallmark of clinical expertise [26]. Since then, studies have shown that, experienced nurses rely on pattern recognition and holistic cue inte­ gration to make rapid and accurate assessments in com­ plex clinical environments [27, 28]. Qualitative evidence revealed that nurses frequently sense patient deteriora­ tion based on subtle, nonverbal cues-such as changes in skin tone, restlessness, or "not looking right"-even before objective vital signs reveal abnormalities. This intuitive awareness has been described as a form of embodied, tacit knowledge that complements analytical reasoning [29-31]. The present study adds quantitative evidence sup­ porting the notion that intuitive recognition can be reliably measured. The unidimensional factor struc­ ture of the Turkish NIPDS aligns with theoretical per­ spectives that conceptualize intuition as an integrated cognitive-perceptual process rather than discrete sen­ sory, emotional, or cognitive domains [8]. The internal consistency results (Cronbach's α = 0.797) indicate that the Turkish NIPDS achieves satisfactory reliability according to the widely accepted threshold for new instruments (≥ 0.70) [21]. The corrected item-total correlations, all above 0.77, demonstrate that each item contributes meaningfully to the total construct and that there is strong homogeneity among the nine items. These findings suggest that the items are theoretically coher­ ent and empirically unified in measuring nurses' intuitive perception of deterioration. Exploratory factor analysis yielded a one-factor solu­ tion accounting for 85.52% of total variance, supported by a high Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO = 0.934) value and significant Bartlett's test of sphericity. Factor loadings ranging between 0.805 and 0.897 indicate that all items had substantial loadings on the single latent factor. This outcome reinforces the theoretical assumption that intu­ ition, in the context of clinical deterioration, represents a unified construct encompassing behavioral, perceptual, and affective cues perceived by nurses. Criterion validity analysis demonstrated a weak but sta­ tistically significant positive correlation between NIPDS and NEWS scores. Although the magnitude of the corre­ lation was modest, this result is conceptually meaningful because the two tools capture distinct yet complemen­ tary constructs. Combining intuition with objective data may improve early recognition. The NIPDS may comple­ ment NEWS by capturing nurses' intuitive perceptions of early decline, whereas NEWS quantifies physiological deterioration using objective vital-sign parameters [32]. The NIPDS reflects nurses' intuitive perception of early clinical decline, whereas the NEWS quantifies physiolog­ ical derangement using objective vital-sign parameters [22]. These factors can result in missed or delayed recognition of patient deterioration and inappropriate management. Incorporating the Nurse Intuition Patient Deteriora­ tion Scale (NIPDS) alongside NEWS may help mitigate these risks by supporting nurses' intuitive judgments and enhancing early recognition of clinical deterioration [33]. Practically, the Turkish version of the NIPDS offers a valuable tool for both educational and clinical appli­ cations. In nursing education, it can be employed to enhance students' self-awareness of intuitive reasoning and to facilitate reflection on non-analytical aspects of clinical judgment. In practice, the instrument can com­ plement early warning systems and clinical observation tools to strengthen nurses' situational awareness and early detection of deterioration. Integrating the NIPDS into clinical protocols could encourage nurses to system­ atically record intuitive perceptions, fostering interdisci­ plinary communication and early escalation of care. Furthermore, the validated instrument can serve as a foundation for research exploring how intuition inter­ acts with other predictors of patient outcomes, such as surveillance behaviors, teamwork, and decision-making. Its inclusion in predictive modeling, digital monitoring systems, or artificial intelligence-based early warning platforms could potentially improve the sensitivity and timeliness of deterioration detection. In this way, intu­ ition becomes not merely a subjective "gut feeling" but a measurable element within evidence-based patient safety systems. Importantly, this is the first adaptation and validation of the NIPDS in the Turkish context, thereby expanding the instrument's applicability for international comparative research on nurse intuition and patient dete­ rioration. The validation of this tool in Turkish enables its use for both research and clinical applications within local healthcare contexts. Limitations This study has some limitations that should be acknowl­ edged. The sample was limited to nurses from a single private tertiary teaching and research hospital, which may restrict generalizability to other settings, such as public hospitals. The methodological design did not allow the assessment of predictive validity or the stability of the scale over time. Additionally, data were collected using self-reported questionnaires, which may have introduced response bias. Although internal consistency was satisfactory, test-retest reliability was not evaluated and should be examined in future studies. Finally, confir­ matory factor analysis was not performed in this study; therefore, future studies could conduct confirmatory fac­ tor analysis to further validate the factor structure. Finally, while the correlation between NIPDS and NEWS supports criterion validity, further research is needed to explore predictive associations with actual clinical outcomes, such as unplanned ICU admissions or cardiac arrest events, as during our data collection period, none of these events were recorded for any of the participant patients. Future directions Future studies should aim to replicate these findings in larger and more diverse samples to verify the generaliz­ ability of the Turkish NIPDS. Cross-cultural validations in other languages and healthcare contexts are also rec­ ommended to establish international comparability. Lon­ gitudinal studies could examine whether higher NIPDS scores predict adverse patient outcomes or correlate with recognition of and intervention in clinical deterioration. Integrating the NIPDS into digital health systems such as electronic health records (EHRs) could further expand its practical value. Moreover, studies combining quantita­ tive and qualitative approaches may enhance understand­ ing of how intuition interacts with clinical reasoning, emotional intelligence, and contextual factors in nursing practice.

chunk_text: The NIPDS has been shown to effectively quantify intu­ ition-an inherently abstract, experience-based form of clinical reasoning-into a quantifiable construct that can be systematically evaluated. Implementing a psychometrically sound instrument to measure intuitive judgment is an important step that will help nurses integrate the knowledge they gain through their experiences into patient safety practices and early warning systems. The Turkish version of the Nurse Intuition Patient Deterioration Scale demonstrated strong psychomet­ ric properties, confirming its reliability, construct valid­ ity, and criterion-related validity. The findings suggest intuition as a measurable and meaningful component of nurses' clinical assessment of patient deterioration. This study contributes to the theoretical advancement of nursing science by bridging the divide between intui­ tive expertise and empirical measurement. In practice, the NIPDS can serve as an evidence-based instrument to support clinical decision-making, guide educational Page 9 of 10 Pamir Aksoy et al. BMC Nursing (2026) 25:212 interventions, and inform patient safety strategies. Rec­ ognizing and validating the role of intuition not only honors the experiential foundation of nursing practice but also enhances the precision, responsiveness, and humanity of patient care.
